summary: Describes how a BEEP session is mapped onto a single TCP connection. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3081 says how to run BEEP, a protocol for exchanging messages over numbered channels, on an ordinary TCP connection. One TCP connection carries one BEEP session. Because several channels can share that connection, BEEP keeps a separate flow-control window for each channel, so one busy channel cannot starve the others.

subtitle: How to run a BEEP session, with its numbered channels, over one ordinary TCP connection.

tldr.problem: BEEP exchanges messages over several numbered channels at once, but a TCP connection only controls the flow of the whole connection, so one busy channel could starve the others or deadlock the session.
tldr.mechanism: One TCP connection carries one BEEP session, with the passive opener named the listener and the active opener the initiator. BEEP keeps its own flow control: every channel has a sliding window of payload octets, started at 4096 and advertised to the peer in SEQ frames.
tldr.outcome: The result is that BEEP can run over a single TCP connection without one channel taking over, with rules for segmentation, round-robin sending between channels and window sizes based on real buffer space. The memo adds no security rules of its own.

facts.label: Sequence number space
facts.value: 0 to 4294967295, arithmetic modulo 2 to the power of 32

facts.label: Frame size guideline
facts.value: Two-thirds of TCP's negotiated maximum segment size

today: RFC 3081 is a Proposed Standard from March 2001 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It is one half of a pair: RFC 3080 defines the BEEP core that this memo maps onto TCP, and this memo says how the sessions, channels and frames of that core travel over a single TCP connection.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo describes how a BEEP session, the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol, is mapped onto a single TCP connection. The mapping requirements themselves are explained in section 2.5 of the BEEP core specification, RFC 3080.

The mapping has two halves. Session management maps onto the TCP connection calls, so that one TCP connection is one BEEP session. Message exchange maps onto the TCP send and receive calls, with one addition: BEEP keeps its own flow control per channel, because TCP only controls the flow of a whole connection and several BEEP channels can be in use at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 3081 says how to run BEEP, a protocol for exchanging messages over numbered channels, on an ordinary TCP connection. One TCP connection carries one BEEP session, and BEEP adds its own per-channel flow control on top of TCP's.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
The mapping of BEEP session management onto the TCP service is straightforward. A BEEP session is established when a TCP connection is established between two BEEP peers. The peer that issues a passive TCP OPEN call is the listener, and the peer that issues an active TCP OPEN call is the initiator.

A simultaneous TCP OPEN would result in both BEEP peers believing they are the initiator, and neither peer would be able to start any channels. Because of this, services based on BEEP must be designed so that simultaneous TCP OPENs cannot occur.

If both peers agree to release a BEEP session, the peer sending the ok reply immediately issues the TCP CLOSE call. Upon receiving the reply, the other peer immediately issues the TCP CLOSE call as well. A BEEP session is terminated when either peer issues the TCP ABORT call, and the TCP connection is subsequently aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: One TCP connection is one BEEP session. The side that accepts the connection is the listener and the side that dials is the initiator, and a service must make sure that both sides never dial at once, or neither can open a channel.

sections.title: Message Exchange
sections.content:
The mapping of BEEP exchanges onto the TCP service is less straightforward. Messages are reliably sent and received using TCP's SEND and RECEIVE calls, which also provides ordered delivery of messages on the same channel.

Although TCP imposes flow control on a per-connection basis, if multiple channels are simultaneously in use on a BEEP session, BEEP must provide a mechanism to avoid starvation and deadlock. To achieve this, BEEP re-introduces a mechanism used by TCP: window-based flow control. Each channel has a sliding window that indicates the number of payload octets that a peer may transmit before receiving further permission.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages travel as ordinary reliable TCP data, in order within a channel. Because several channels can share one connection, BEEP keeps a separate window for each channel, so one busy channel cannot starve the others or deadlock the session.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Channel Creation
sections.content:
Every payload octet sent in each direction on a channel has an associated sequence number. Numbering of payload octets within a data frame is such that the first payload octet is the lowest numbered, and the following payload octets are numbered consecutively.

The actual sequence number space is finite, though very large, ranging from 0 to 4294967295, which is two to the power of 32 minus 1. Since the space is finite, all arithmetic dealing with sequence numbers is performed modulo that same power of 32. That unsigned arithmetic preserves the relationship of sequence numbers as they cycle from the maximum back to zero again.

When a channel is created, the sequence number associated with the first payload octet of the first data frame is 0, and the initial window size for that channel is 4096 octets. After channel creation, a BEEP peer may update the window size by sending a SEQ frame.

If a BEEP peer is asked to create a channel and it is unable to allocate at least 4096 octets for that channel, it must decline creation of the channel. Similarly, during establishment of the BEEP session, if the peer acting in the listening role is unable to allocate at least 4096 octets for channel 0, then it must return a negative reply instead of a greeting.
sections.plainLanguage: Each byte sent on a channel is numbered, and the numbers run from 0 to 4294967295 and then start again. A new channel starts at zero and is given a window of 4096 bytes, so a peer that cannot find that much buffer space has to refuse the channel.

sections.title: The SEQ Frame
sections.content:
As an application accepts responsibility for incoming data frames, its BEEP peer should send SEQ frames to advertise a new window. The ABNF for a SEQ frame is:

seq    = "SEQ" SP channel SP ackno SP window CR LF
ackno  = seqno
window = size

The frame has three parameters. The channel number says which channel the frame is about. The acknowledgement number is the value of the next sequence number that the sender is expecting to receive on that channel. The window size is the number of payload octets, beginning with the one indicated by the acknowledgement number, that the sender is expecting to receive on the channel.

A single space character separates each component, and the frame is terminated with a CRLF pair. When a SEQ frame is received and any of the channel number, acknowledgement number or window size cannot be determined or is invalid, the BEEP session is terminated without generating a response, and it is recommended that a diagnostic entry be logged.
sections.plainLanguage: A SEQ frame is a short line of text that says which channel it is about, which byte the receiver expects next, and how many bytes it is willing to take from there. If any of those three values is wrong, the session is dropped.

sections.title: Sharing the Connection Fairly
sections.content:
The key to successful use of flow control within BEEP is to balance performance and fairness. Large messages should be segmented into frames no larger than two-thirds of TCP's negotiated maximum segment size. Frames for different channels with traffic ready to send should be sent in a round-robin fashion. Each time a frame is received, a SEQ frame should be sent whenever the window size that will be sent is at least one half of the buffer space available to that channel. And if the transport service presents multiple frames to a BEEP peer simultaneously, a single consolidating SEQ frame may be sent.

To avoid pathological interactions with the transport service, it is important that a peer advertise windows based on available buffer space, so that data can be read from the transport service as soon as it is available. SEQ frames for a channel must have higher priority than messages for that channel.

Implementations may wish to provide queue management facilities to the application, such as channel priorities and relative buffer allocations. In particular, an implementation should not allow a given channel to monopolize the underlying transport window, so a slow reader should get small windows. Where possible, implementations should support transport layer APIs that convey congestion information, which let an implementation determine its share of the available bandwidth and be notified of changes in the estimated path bandwidth. A session in which several channels are simultaneously exchanging large messages may have uncertain fairness and progress properties during times of network congestion if the implementation has no access to that information.

Implementors should follow the flow control guidelines in the relevant portions of RFC 1122, bearing in mind that issues such as retransmission, which do interact with flow control in TCP, are not applicable here; only the portions concerning flow control should be implemented. That guidance includes the rule that a receiver should not shrink the window, that is, move the right window edge to the left.
sections.plainLanguage: Because several channels share one connection, the RFC sets out how to share it fairly: keep frames small, take turns between channels, and hand out window space based on real buffer space so that no channel can take over the connection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo has no security rules of its own. It points the reader to section 9 of the BEEP core specification, RFC 3080, for the discussion of security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 3081 adds no security rules of its own. The security discussion lives in the BEEP core specification it builds on.

messages.label: TCP active OPEN
messages.note: The peer that issues the active OPEN is the initiator.

messages.label: TCP connection established
messages.note: The peer that issued the passive OPEN is the listener.

messages.label: TCP CLOSE
messages.note: When both peers agree to release the session, the peer that sends the ok reply issues the TCP CLOSE call immediately.

messages.label: TCP CLOSE
messages.note: On receiving the reply, the other peer immediately issues the TCP CLOSE call too.

messages.label: TCP ABORT
messages.note: Either peer can end the session by issuing the TCP ABORT call, after which the connection is aborted.

data.title: SEQ frame syntax
data.code:
seq    = "SEQ" SP channel SP ackno SP window CR LF
ackno  = seqno
window = size

items.title: Keep frames small
items.text: Segment large messages into frames no larger than two-thirds of TCP's negotiated maximum segment size.

items.title: Take turns
items.text: Send frames for different channels with traffic ready in a round-robin fashion.

items.title: Reopen the window early
items.text: Send a SEQ frame whenever the window to be sent is at least one half of the buffer space available to the channel.

items.title: Offer real space
items.text: Advertise windows from available buffer space, and do not let one channel monopolize the transport window.
